text.p: The chairman of SGS-Thomson Microelectronics NV, Pasquale Pistorio, said on Thursday that he was "extremely confident" on the medium and long-term that his company would outperform the market.
But he declined to comment on suggestions that the group's 1997 full-year profit will be down.

"I cannot make profit forecasts, that is for you to calculate," he said. Financial analysts are considering reducing their 1997 earnings per share estimates, currently at an average of $3.50. In 1996 earnings per share were $4.50.
Pistorio told a news conference that on the medium and long-term he was "extremely confident" that SGS-Thomson would outperfom the market it serves in terms of sales, profit and return on equity.
In the short term, SGS-Thomson expects the third quarter gross margin to be stable compared to the 38.5 percent of the second quarter of 1997.
In 1998, the margin would return to a range of 40 to 42 percent. "In good times the margin range is between 40 and 42 percent. In 1998 we will be in that range," he said.
The operating profit in the first half of 1997 stood at 12 percent of sales which Pistorio called "for the cycle not too bad" and said it had "stablised at the bottom."
Pistorio said the company expected the world semiconductor market, in dollar terms, to grow between five and seven percent in 1997.
This is in line with a May forecast of seven percent but lower than the six to eight percent range forecast by Motorola Inc on July 9.

Pistorio said that the market had hit the bottom of the cycle in February and was at the start of a new cycle. He noted chipmakers were buying equipment and extending capacity ahead of the expected upturn, which meant that excess capcity would last a bit longer.
He said average selling prices were between 10 and 25 percent below their second quarter of 1996 level, but these prices were stabilising for many products.
Of SGS-Thomson's total sales, 57 percent was made up of high-margin differentiated products. Pistorio said this would be 60 percent at the year-end.
He said that the dollar's strength was making the company more competitive and was reducing its cost base but the influence on the bottom line was very small.
